claims.text: Oxidation resistance and material integrity in multiprincipal-element alloys are governed by preferential diffusion and surface segregation of reactive elements.
Al, Cr, and Ti can act as reactive elements in the proposed oxidation mechanism.
Reactive-element enrichment promotes formation of a continuous, self-healing surface oxide scale.
The initial alloy has a homogeneous distribution of reactive and non-reactive elements.
High-temperature oxidizing exposure with cyclic thermal loading produces a continuous, adherent, reactive-element-enriched oxide scale.
Reactive elements diffuse to the alloy surface under high-temperature oxidizing conditions.
Reactive elements oxidize rapidly at the surface to form a compact, self-healing oxide scale.
The compact oxide scale limits further oxygen ingress and material degradation.
Segregation dynamics inherent to multiprincipal-element alloys enhance protective-scale formation.
Standard or enhanced reactive-element content will produce a more uniform and coherent protective scale than deliberately reduced reactive-element content.
Standard or enhanced reactive-element content will result in lower oxidation mass gain than reduced reactive-element content.
Standard or enhanced reactive-element content will preserve mechanical integrity better than reduced reactive-element content during long-term oxidation.
The proposed behavior should hold when oxidation is the primary degradation mechanism, including oxidizing atmospheres above approximately 800°C.
At lower temperatures or under non-oxidizing conditions, degradation mechanisms other than high-temperature oxidation may dominate.
Differences in oxide morphology and the effects of other alloying elements may alter the response.
Two alloys differing in reactive-element content can be compared through identical cyclic oxidation tests at approximately 900°C for about 100 hours.

Failure of the standard or enhanced-reactive-element alloy to show lower mass gain, improved scale continuity, and better integrity relative to the reduced-content alloy would falsify the proposed governing mechanism.
